Model B must definitely be the better model here, precisely because its AUC value is lower
explanation: AUC reflects a model's overall ranking quality across all thresholds, not just performance at one fixed cutoff, so a higher AUC indicates generally stronger discrimination between classes even when accuracy at a single threshold looks comparable.

q: A plot of training loss versus epoch for a logistic regression model trained with gradient descent shows the loss steadily decreasing and then leveling off, forming a smooth, flattening curve. What does this pattern typically indicate?
options: The model is converging toward a minimum of the convex cross-entropy loss, with diminishing improvement as it approaches it
The model is overfitting severely and the training loss curve should instead be increasing
The learning rate must actually have been set to zero, since the loss eventually stops changing at all
Gradient descent has clearly failed here and must be restarted using a different weight initialization
explanation: A smooth, flattening loss curve is the expected signature of gradient descent converging toward the minimum of a convex loss surface, with updates producing smaller and smaller improvements as the minimum is approached.

q: What is the value of the sigmoid function's derivative at z=0, and why is this property useful during gradient-based training?
options: The derivative is at its maximum value (0.25) at z=0, giving the strongest gradient signal exactly where the model is most uncertain

The derivative is exactly zero at z=0 in this case, so essentially no learning occurs anywhere near the decision boundary, which would make gradient descent stall precisely where classification is hardest
The derivative is undefined at z=0 because the function is discontinuous there
The derivative of the sigmoid equals exactly 1 at every single value of z, including z=0
explanation: The sigmoid's derivative, sigmoid(z)*(1-sigmoid(z)), is maximized at z=0 where sigmoid(z)=0.5, giving the strongest gradient signal for points near the decision boundary, which is often where learning matters most.

q: A dataset for predicting disease presence (0/1) has one patient with an extremely high value for a lab feature compared to the rest of the cohort. A plain linear regression fit (thresholded at 0.5) misclassifies several otherwise-clear-cut patients because of this one patient. What does this scenario illustrate about linear regression for classification?
options: Linear regression's squared-error objective is sensitive to outliers, which can distort the fitted line and shift the threshold for unrelated points
Linear regression simply cannot be used at all whenever any single feature contains large numeric values

This behavior actually shows that linear regression is more robust to outliers than logistic regression is in general, since the squared-error line visibly shifted while the classification rule stayed fixed
This particular issue is claimed to only occur if the dataset happens to have fewer than 10 rows total
explanation: Squared-error minimization weights large deviations heavily, so a single extreme point can pull the fitted regression line and shift where it crosses the classification threshold, misclassifying other points \u2014 a key motivation for using logistic regression instead.

q: What is the bug in the code below, given that the dataset's raw CSV file has no header row?
options: The names=columns argument is missing from read_csv, so pandas will treat the first data row as the header and auto-generate integer column names instead
pd.read_csv is claimed to never be usable for loading a file directly from a URL under any circumstances
The columns list has too many entries and pandas will raise a length-mismatch error

CSV files that lack header rows are claimed to never be loadable by pandas under any circumstances at all, regardless of arguments passed, meaning read_csv would need an entirely different library just to open this file
explanation: Without passing names=columns (or header=None), pandas defaults to using the first row of data as column headers and may auto-generate integer names, silently losing the intended column labels and the first data row.

q: Why is logistic regression sometimes described as a type of generalized linear model (GLM)?
options: It models a transformed version of the target's expectation (the log-odds) as a linear function of the input features, which is the defining idea of a GLM
It supposedly has no linear components anywhere at all in its underlying mathematical formulation

GLM is simply just another informal name used for any model that happens to be trained using ordinary gradient descent, regardless of what link function, if any, connects its linear predictor to the response
It is called a GLM only because its name happens to contain the word "regression" in it
explanation: Generalized linear models combine a linear predictor with a link function connecting it to the expected value of the response; logistic regression uses the logit as its link function, relating the log-odds linearly to the features.

q: A retail churn model with L2 regularization is evaluated at several regularization strengths, and the training/validation accuracy curves are plotted against model complexity. Near one end of the complexity scale, both curves show low accuracy; near the other end, training accuracy approaches 100% while validation accuracy drops. What does the region between these two extremes represent?
options: The region of good generalization, where the model is complex enough to capture real patterns but not so complex that it starts fitting noise
A region that should never be chosen at all because it always has lower training accuracy than every other region on the curve, even though validation accuracy there is actually at its highest point
The region in the middle where the model's predictions supposedly become undefined entirely
A region that exists only in theory and cannot be identified using real validation data
explanation: Between underfitting (both curves low) and overfitting (training high, validation low) lies a region of appropriate complexity where the model generalizes best; this sweet spot is typically what hyperparameter tuning via cross-validation aims to find.

q: Compared to one-vs-rest, what is a key characteristic of the multinomial (softmax) approach to multiclass logistic regression?
options: It fits a single unified model that jointly produces normalized probabilities across all classes at once, rather than combining separately trained binary classifiers
It can supposedly only ever be used when there are exactly two possible classes to predict
It is said to require training a completely separate neural network model from scratch for each individual class, unlike the single unified softmax model it is actually being compared against here
It produces class probabilities that are claimed not to need summing to 1 across all classes
explanation: Multinomial logistic regression directly models the probabilities of all classes jointly using the softmax function within a single optimization, as opposed to one-vs-rest, which trains independent binary classifiers and combines their outputs afterward.

q: What does the F1 score represent for a binary classifier?
options: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing both into a single metric
The simple arithmetic average computed between accuracy and AUC for the model
The total raw count of all examples that were correctly classified by the model
The variance of the predicted probabilities across all test examples
explanation: F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, giving a single balanced measure that penalizes models which sacrifice one metric heavily to improve the other.

q: A logistic regression model trained on credit data uses only raw, untransformed numeric features (income, debt ratio, age) and achieves a straight-line decision boundary that separates most but not all defaulters from non-defaulters. Why can't increasing the regularization strength alone fix a boundary shape that is fundamentally too simple for the data?
options: Regularization controls how much coefficients shrink, not the functional form of the boundary; a linear boundary stays linear unless the feature set itself changes
Increasing regularization strength always converts a linear boundary into a curved one automatically
Regularization strength and decision boundary shape are claimed to be mathematically the exact same quantity

The boundary's shape is said to depend only on the choice of optimizer algorithm used, never on regularization strength or the input features themselves, regardless of what transformations are engineered
explanation: Regularization adjusts the magnitude of the coefficients to control overfitting, but it does not change the functional form of the model; without adding transformed or interaction features, the decision boundary in the original feature space remains linear no matter how C or lambda is tuned.

q: Two fraud-detection models are compared using total cross-entropy loss on the same test set. Model A has a lower total loss than Model B, even though both have identical accuracy. What does this most likely mean?
options: Model A's predicted probabilities are generally better calibrated, closer to 0 or 1 for the correct class, than Model B's, even though both cross the same threshold similarly often

Model A must simply have been fit with a lower regularization strength than Model B in every single possible case, since weaker regularization is mistakenly assumed to always directly lower the total cross-entropy loss on held-out data
Cross-entropy loss and accuracy always move together, so this situation could not actually occur
Model B must be using a different loss function internally, making the comparison invalid
explanation: Cross-entropy loss rewards confident, well-calibrated correct predictions and penalizes weakly-confident ones even when they fall on the correct side of the threshold, so two models can have the same accuracy but differ in total loss based on how well-calibrated their probabilities are.

q: In scikit-learn, what is the default penalty type applied by LogisticRegression if the penalty parameter is left unspecified?
options: L2 regularization
L1 regularization
No regularization (penalty=None) is always the default
Elastic net combining L1 and L2 equally
explanation: Scikit-learn's LogisticRegression defaults to L2 regularization (penalty="l2") with C=1.0, unless a different penalty or regularization strength is explicitly specified.

q: A company trains a logistic regression model on streaming transaction data arriving continuously and wants to update the model incrementally without retraining from scratch on the full history each time. Which optimization approach best supports this incremental update pattern?
options: Stochastic gradient descent, which can update the weights using one (or a few) new examples at a time
A closed-form normal equation solved once on the full historical dataset
An exhaustive grid search performed over all possible weight combinations for the model
Running k-means clustering directly on the raw transaction features instead of classifying them
explanation: Stochastic gradient descent updates weights incrementally using individual or small batches of examples, making it naturally suited to streaming or online learning settings where retraining on the full history each time is impractical.

q: Which of the following is a practical strategy for reducing multicollinearity among input features before fitting logistic regression, aside from applying regularization?
options: Combining or removing some of the highly correlated features, e.g. via dimensionality reduction or domain-driven feature selection
Simply increasing the learning rate used during gradient descent training of the model
Switching the activation function entirely from sigmoid over to a hard step function
Deliberately adding even more highly correlated features in an attempt to balance out the ones already present, even though this would only make the multicollinearity problem measurably worse
explanation: Beyond regularization, multicollinearity can be addressed by removing or combining redundant correlated features (e.g. through domain knowledge or techniques like PCA), reducing the redundancy that destabilizes coefficient estimates.
